title: How To Bring New Students Into Your Peaceful Classroom ful-classroom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns that a new student's initially calm demeanor can be deceptive, since habits and behaviors permitted at their previous school will eventually resurface if not proactively addressed. He recommends against assuming students will simply figure things out by observing peers, laying out instead a structured ten-minute conference to orient every new arrival. The steps include setting a serious tone, clearly stating the behavioral expectation, explaining each class rule and its purpose, laying out the consequence system, promising consistent enforcement, reviewing the parent information packet together, and securing signatures from both student and parent. He notes that modeling isn't part of the process, since new students absorb classroom norms quickly just by watching classmates — provided the classroom's routines and procedures are already solid. The piece frames a well-run classroom's intrinsic appeal as the real force that draws new students, even difficult ones, into alignment without further intervention.
points: A new student's calm first days can be misleading; prior habits typically resurface if expectations aren't proactively addressed.
A structured ten-minute conference — not left to peer modeling alone — should orient every new student to the classroom's expectations.
The conference should cover the core expectation, the purpose behind each rule, the consequence system, and a commitment to consistent enforcement.
Reviewing and signing the parent information packet together, plus contacting the parent, helps secure buy-in and trust.
A genuinely peaceful, well-run classroom's intrinsic appeal is what ultimately draws even difficult new students into alignment.
quotes: Although often calm and quiet in the beginning, whatever habits and behaviors were permitted at their previous school will eventually bubble to the surface.
Typically, a ten minute conference with the new student is all that is needed to ensure a peaceful transition.
Very simply and directly state that in your classroom students behave, and that will be expected of them as well.
You’ll then make the same promise you make to all of your students that you will follow your classroom management plan to a tee.
This is a critical step in earning their trust and support of you and your program.
If your classroom management is solid, and you’re steadfast in your consistency, even the most difficult new students fall in line without you having to say another word.
They experience the intrinsic allure of a happy and productive classroom. And they want to be part of it too.
